/sermons/awake-in-the-dark.title: Awake in the dark | Morrow Church Sermons
/sermons/awake-in-the-dark.description: Paul writes to people anxious about the future. Instead of a timetable, he gives them a way to live: awake, sober and encouraging one another.
p: Letters to a Young Church, part 4
Paul writes to people anxious about the future. Instead of a timetable, he gives them a way to live: awake, sober and encouraging one another.

The Thessalonians want dates. Paul gives them an identity instead. They are children of the light, so they do not need to be surprised or afraid. What they need is to stay awake to what God is doing right now.
“Therefore encourage one another and build each other up, just as in fact you are doing.”
Hope, in this letter, is not a feeling about tomorrow. It is a practice for today: faith and love worn like armor, and friends who keep reminding each other who they are.
What worries about the future are taking up the most room in your head?
What helps you stay awake to God in an ordinary week?
Who could you encourage by name before Sunday?
Read Romans 13:11-14 alongside this passage and look for the shared images of night and morning.

/sermons/a-quiet-life.title: A quiet life | Morrow Church Sermons
/sermons/a-quiet-life.description: Paul tells a young, excited church to make it their ambition to live quietly, mind their own business and work with their hands. It is more radical than it sounds.
p: Letters to a Young Church, part 5
Paul tells a young, excited church to make it their ambition to live quietly, mind their own business and work with their hands. It is more radical than it sounds.

The church in Thessalonica is already known for its love. Paul does not ask them for something new. He asks them to keep going, and to do it in an unexpected direction: quieter, steadier and more ordinary.
“Make it your ambition to lead a quiet life: You should mind your own business and work with your hands.”

In a culture that rewards being seen, Paul describes faith that looks like showing up for work, paying your bills and treating your neighbors well. The quiet life is not a small life. It is a life that wins the respect of outsiders without trying to.
What would change if your ambition were a quiet life rather than a notable one?
Where does your work, paid or unpaid, already serve your neighbors?
Who has shown you what steady faithfulness looks like?
Read all of 1 Thessalonians in one sitting. It takes about fifteen minutes.

/sermons/a-table-in-the-tax-office.title: A table in the tax office | Morrow Church Sermons
/sermons/a-table-in-the-tax-office.description: Jesus calls a tax collector named Levi, and Levi throws a party. The guest list is the scandal, and the scandal is the point.
h1: A table in the tax office
p: A table in the tax office
Jesus calls a tax collector named Levi, and Levi throws a party. The guest list is the scandal, and the scandal is the point.

Levi collects taxes for Rome, which makes him rich and widely disliked. Jesus walks past his booth, says two words, and Levi leaves everything behind. The first thing he does as a follower of Jesus is host a very large dinner for all his friends.
“It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.”

The religious leaders complain about the company Jesus keeps. Jesus does not argue about whether the guests are sinners. He simply says that this is exactly who he came for, which turns out to include the people doing the complaining.
Who would make you uncomfortable at a dinner with Jesus?
What would it look like to throw a Levi party with the friends you already have?
Which do you identify with more right now: Levi, his friends or the critics?
Read Luke 15:1-2 and the three stories that follow. They answer the same complaint.

/sermons/bread-for-five-thousand.title: Bread for five thousand | Morrow Church Sermons
/sermons/bread-for-five-thousand.description: The disciples want to send the crowd home before dinner. Jesus hands them five loaves, two fish and a job they are not qualified for.
p: The disciples want to send the crowd home before dinner. Jesus hands them five loaves, two fish and a job they are not qualified for.

The day has been long and the place is remote. The disciples have a sensible plan: send everyone into the villages to find food. Jesus answers with a sentence that still makes leaders nervous: “You give them something to eat.”
“Taking the five loaves and the two fish and looking up to heaven, he gave thanks and broke them.”

Nothing in the story starts with abundance. It starts with not enough, offered anyway. Jesus blesses it, breaks it and gives it back to the disciples to pass around. Twelve baskets of leftovers suggest that the table was never the problem.
Where are you tempted to send people away because you feel you have too little to offer?
What are your five loaves and two fish this season?
How could your home group feed someone this month, literally or otherwise?
Compare this meal with the Last Supper in Luke 22:14-20. Notice the same four verbs: took, blessed, broke, gave.

/sermons/the-dinner-that-went-sideways.title: The dinner that went sideways | Morrow Church Sermons
/sermons/the-dinner-that-went-sideways.description: A respectable dinner turns awkward when an uninvited woman kneels at Jesus’ feet. Simon sees a scandal. Jesus sees someone who has been forgiven much.
p: A respectable dinner turns awkward when an uninvited woman kneels at Jesus’ feet. Simon sees a scandal. Jesus sees someone who has been forgiven much.

Simon the Pharisee has invited Jesus to dinner, probably to size him up. Then a woman with a reputation walks in, weeps over Jesus’ feet and dries them with her hair. Every guest at that table knows exactly what should happen next, and Jesus does none of it.
“Therefore I tell you, her many sins have been forgiven, as her great love has shown.”

Jesus tells a short story about two debts, one large and one small, and lets Simon answer his own question. The point lands gently but firmly: the people who know how much they have been forgiven are the ones who love most freely.
When have you been more like Simon than you would like to admit?
What makes it hard to receive forgiveness without trying to earn it back?
Who in your life is treated like the woman at this dinner?
Read Luke 7 and 8 together and notice how often Jesus lets people interrupt him.

/sermons/who-gets-a-seat.title: Who gets a seat? | Morrow Church Sermons
/sermons/who-gets-a-seat.description: At a dinner party, Jesus watches the guests jostle for the good chairs. Then he turns to the host with a stranger guest list in mind.
p: At a dinner party, Jesus watches the guests jostle for the good chairs. Then he turns to the host with a stranger guest list in mind.

In Jesus’ world, your place at the table announced your place in town. He doesn’t lecture the guests so much as hand them an exit from the contest: choose the lowest chair and let the host decide what you’re worth. Then he tells the host that the whole invitation list needs turning over.
“But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed.”

This isn’t etiquette advice. It is a glimpse of God’s kingdom, where the guests who can never return the favor are seated first, and where each of us eventually realizes we were the ones brought in from the road.
Where do you catch yourself angling for the better chair, at work, online or in the family?
Who could never repay you? What would an invitation to them look like this month?
Read Luke 14:21-23 aloud. Which person in the story feels most like you right now?
Name one person who needs a place at your table, and pray for them together.
Read all of Luke 14 in one go, then turn to Isaiah 25:6-9 for the banquet Jesus seems to be echoing.

/about.title: About Morrow Church | Our Story, Beliefs and Leadership
/about.description: Morrow Church began as a porch supper in 2015 and now meets in a 1927 firehouse in West Asheville. Our story, beliefs and leadership.
h2: From a back porch to old Station 4.
The people with keys to the bay doors.
p: Morrow began in 2015 with nine people and a borrowed table. A decade later we still think the best conversations happen over food.

Daniel and Imani Okoro started hosting a Sunday supper on their back porch off Brevard Road, with a Bible open between the casseroles. By the second summer the porch was sagging, and the guest list had outgrown the street.

In 2020 the congregation bought Station 4, a 1927 firehouse on Haywood Road that had sat empty for years. Volunteers rewired it, patched the hose tower and kept the brass pole. Today several hundred people call Morrow home, and on warm Sundays the bay doors still roll open to the sidewalk.
Behind every number below is someone we can point to across the room on a Sunday.
The youngest was eleven, the oldest eighty-one.
Spread from Haw Creek to Candler.
Sample figures. Swap in your church’s own numbers.
Morrow is a nondenominational church that stands on the Apostles’ and Nicene Creeds. In everyday words, it looks like this.
Everything that exists was made on purpose by a God who keeps showing up for it.
Jesus took our place on the cross and walked out of the grave. In him we find forgiveness and a fresh start.
Through the Bible, God speaks to ordinary people. We study it out loud, wrestle with it and try to live by it.
Grace can’t be earned. You are free to watch, ask and doubt for as long as you need.
Church is a people more than a program. That means shared meals, hard conversations and turning up for one another.
West Asheville should be a kinder place because Morrow is on Haywood Road.
Three of us are on staff. Everything else at Morrow runs on volunteers who came once and kept coming.
Lead Pastor. Former line cook who still runs the Tuesday Table stove.
Pastor of Care. Hospital chaplain for twenty years, now our resident listener.
Students and Young Adults. Builds the fires and somehow remembers every name.
Try one Sunday. If it’s not your place, the coffee was still on us.
No sign-up and no dress code. The bay doors open at 9.
